content.title: About
content.content: Lemon-butter sauce is a classic sauce made from butter, fresh lemon juice, grated zest, salt, and sometimes herbs. It offers a bright, refreshing flavor with a balance of acidity and richness, perfect for fish, seafood, chicken, and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce originated in French cuisine in the 19th century as a variation of classic beurre blanc with added lemon.
Lemon juice not only adds flavor but also stabilizes the emulsion, preventing the butter from separating.
Traditionally the sauce is cooked over low heat while whisking constantly to keep the butter from curdling.
Finely chopped parsley or dill can be added for extra aroma.
Lemon‑butter sauce is often served in small ramekins to keep it warm.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Lemon juice is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and provides antioxidant benefits.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Butter contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: The acidity of lemon stimulates bile production, aiding the digestion of fats.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The sauce contains virtually no carbohydrates, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter provides vitamins A, D, E, and K, essential for various bodily functions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Butter is calorie‑dense; excessive consumption may lead to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from butter.

items.title: Acidic irritation
items.content: Lemon acidity can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Allergy to citrus
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to citrus fruits, causing skin reactions or swelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sauce warm, drizzling it over baked fish, seafood, chicken breasts, or vegetables. It also works as a dip for breadsticks or can be tossed with pasta for a light buttery‑lemon flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Gently reheat over low heat while stirring before serving to re‑emulsify.
